newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's new government faces brief honeymoon.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's new government faces brief honeymoon.

text.p: Turkey's new Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz, heading a right-left minority coalition, faces only a brief honeymoon as he seeks to erase the legacy of social and political tensions left behind by his Islamist predecessor.

But factional timebombs within his secularist camp, the enduring power in parliament of the Islamists, now back in opposition, and Turkey's deepest economic and social problems leave Yilmaz with precious room for manoeuvre.
"In the West we talk about the 100 days' grace period for a new administration," said one foreign diplomat.
"Given the scope of Turkey's problems, that may prove too generous."

The conservative Yilmaz emerged on Saturday with a comfortable vote of confidence, 281-256, but not before a near-riot in parliament as secularist and Islamist MPs exchanged heated insults and even a flurry of punches.

The parliamentary brawl, mirroring the deep divide in this overwhelmingly Moslem but officially secular country, underscores the stakes for Yilmaz, a cautious, deliberate leader now in his third tenure as prime minister.
"The fifty-fifth government is the last chance for Turkey," said Refik Baydur, chairman of the Confederation of Turkish Employers' Unions.
"The people have behaved reasonably at a time of considerable political instability," he told reporters in the western port city of Izmir.

Saturday's vote of confidence capped more than a year of political and social instability that saw the modern republic's first Islamist government under Necmettin Erbakan clash openly with the powerful, secularist armed forces.

Now, Yilmaz must ease the army out of the political arena and soothe social tensions before he can focus on Turkey's daunting problems, most notably chronic inflation of around 75 percent, maldistribution of income and political stagnation.

"This is an opportunity to create the foundation for a normalisation of politics in Turkey and for the necessary structural reforms in political organisations," columnist Hasan Cemal wrote in the big secularist daily Sabah.
For his part, Yilmaz made it clear he would stick to his secularist principles.
"You can sleep peacefully," he wrote on Sunday in a book of condolences at the tomb of Kemal Ataturk, founder of modern Turkey and himself a fierce secularist.
But can his minority government juggle the competing claims in a largely traditional society seeking its place in the modern world?
Already, he is facing demands for early elections from a key social democratic party, which is backing the coalition from outside the government.

Islamist leader Erbakan, confident he will win any fresh elections, predicted on Saturday the new government's days were numbered and warned it was setting the country on the road to "chaos and confusion."

And parliamentary procedure means Yilmaz's new hold on power does not extend to the control of some important parliamentary committees where the Islamists and their conservative allies could still frustrate his secularist agenda.
"This government has a limited amount of time," said commentator Sedat Ergin of the Hurriyet newspaper.
"Hence, it is doubtful that it will be able to deal with the huge problems which have been hanging over Turkey for years."
